Unit 7: Natural Selection

7.17.27.37.47.5 7.67.77.87.97.10 7.117.127.13 TablesTraps
📋 All of Unit 7 in one place — the biggest unit, so scan quickly by bolded term. Use the population-shift animation to lock in how natural selection changes allele frequencies before your test.
7.1

Introduction to Natural Selection

  • Darwin: individuals with advantageous heritable traits survive/reproduce more.
  • Lamarck (incorrect): proposed traits acquired during life could be inherited — disproven by modern genetics (only germline DNA changes are heritable).
The peppered moth.
7.2

Natural Selection

  • Requires heritable variation + differential fitness (survival/reproduction advantage).
  • Over generations, advantageous alleles become more common → allele frequencies shift.
FitnessAdaptation
Selection shifts a trait distribution.
▶ Animation: Natural Selection Shifts a Population
Watch individuals with the advantageous trait (dark) become more common over generations.
7.3

Artificial Selection

  • Humans (not the environment) choose who reproduces, based on desired traits.
  • Broccoli, cabbage, kale all descend from wild mustard via artificial selection.
One species, many vegetables.
7.4

Population Genetics

  • Genetic drift: random allele frequency changes — much stronger in small populations.
  • Gene flow: alleles move between populations via migration.
  • Bottleneck effect (sudden population crash) & founder effect (small group starts new population) are both genetic drift.
Genetic driftGene flowBottleneckFounder effect
A shifting gene pool.
7.5

Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium

  • p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (p²=AA, 2pq=Aa, q²=aa).
  • 5 conditions for equilibrium (no evolution): no mutation, random mating, no selection, huge population (no drift), no gene flow.
Trap: Real populations essentially never meet all 5 conditions — HW is a theoretical baseline, not a real-world default.
Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies.
7.6

Evidence of Evolution

  • Homologous structures: shared underlying structure from common ancestry (different function) — e.g., forelimb bones.
  • Analogous structures: similar function, evolved independently (convergent evolution) — e.g., insect vs. bird wings.
Trap: Homologous = common ancestry; analogous = NOT common ancestry, just similar environmental pressure.
Homologous forelimb bones.
7.7

Common Ancestry

  • Nearly universal genetic code across all life = strong evidence of one shared origin.
  • More DNA/protein sequence similarity → more recent common ancestor.
Shared features across life.
7.8

Continuing Evolution

  • Antibiotic resistance: resistance mutations exist BEFORE exposure; the antibiotic is a selective pressure, not a cause.
  • Evolution is ongoing, observable on human timescales.
Trap: Antibiotics don't create resistance — they select for bacteria that already have it.
Evolution of antibiotic resistance.
7.9

Phylogeny

  • Phylogenetic tree/cladogram: branch points (nodes) = common ancestors.
  • Built using shared derived characteristics (recent, specific traits) — more recent shared node = more closely related.
A phylogenetic tree.
7.10

Speciation

  • Allopatric: geographic barrier splits population, halting gene flow.
  • Sympatric: speciation without geographic separation (e.g., polyploidy).
  • Speciation is complete once reproductive isolation evolves.
Allopatric speciation.
7.11

Extinction

  • Mass extinction: large % of species lost in a short geological time (5 major events, e.g. Permian, Cretaceous/asteroid).
  • Often followed by adaptive radiation as survivors fill newly open niches.
The 5 major mass extinctions.
7.12

Variations in Populations

  • Discrete variation: distinct categories (e.g., blood type), usually 1 gene.
  • Continuous variation: gradual range (e.g., height), polygenic + environment → bell curve.
Discrete vs. continuous variation.
7.13

Origin of Life on Earth

  • Earth formed ~4.6 billion years ago; first life ~3.5 billion years ago.
  • RNA world hypothesis: RNA was likely the first genetic material — it can both store info AND catalyze reactions.
  • Protobionts: simple membrane-bound, cell-like structures — a step toward true cells.
Origin of life timeline.
★

Master Summary Table

ConceptKey Distinction
Homologous vs. analogousShared ancestry (same structure) vs. convergent evolution (same function only)
Allopatric vs. sympatricGeographic separation vs. no geographic separation
Genetic drift vs. natural selectionRandom chance vs. differential fitness
Bottleneck vs. founder effectPopulation crash vs. small group starts new population
Discrete vs. continuous variationDistinct categories (1 gene) vs. gradual range (polygenic)
⚠

Commonly Missed on the Exam

  • Natural selection acts on phenotype, but only changes to genotype are heritable.
  • Genetic drift matters most in small populations — don't apply it casually to large ones.
  • Real populations are never in perfect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
  • Reproductive isolation, not just physical difference, is the key test for speciation.
  • Antibiotic resistance mutations exist before exposure — the drug selects, it doesn't cause.
  • The RNA world hypothesis is compelling because RNA can both store info and catalyze reactions — a dual role DNA and protein split between them.
